item.title: Midterm gains by US gun control activists’ signals decline of gun lobby
item.description: More than 200 people endorsed by Everytown for Gun Safety won state and federal races in loss of dominance for NRA The US midterm elections were not only a big win for the Democrats, but also a huge victory for the gun violence prevention movement, and a sign of the declining power of the once-feared gun lobby. More than 200 people who were endorsed by Everytown for Gun Safety, the prominent umbrella organization for a network of violence prevention groups, won state and federal races, according to data the non-profit shared with the Guardian. And nearly 550 former volunteers for Moms Demand Action, a group that is part of the Everytown network, ran for office as incumbents and first-time candidates. Continue reading...

item.title: Our ‘Paris manifesto’ proposes how to deal with extreme wealth in the AI age | Open letter
item.description: It is possible for democracy to reverse the dynamic of oligarchy. But we must act now The explosion of extreme wealth in the world is the defining social fact of our times. When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001% of our planet’s population equaled 3% of global GDP. Since that time, the wealth held by this tiny group of people – just 3,000 households – has ballooned and now reaches 17% of global GDP. Continue reading...

item.title: Toddlers are not just little people. Their culture deserves respect | Arwa Mahdawi
item.description: Small children do not appreciate it when you join in with their singing or throw away their pee-covered leaves. And only a brute would suggest one of them might be tired Nobody can be good at everything, can they? Take me, for example. While I excel at remembering useless facts, going down online rabbit holes and getting toothpaste on my shirt, my singing is so bad it makes small children cry. This is not hyperbole: my five-year-old has wailed on many occasions throughout her short life because I’ve had the temerity to sing along to various TV show jingles or songs. As it turns out, however, it may not just be the fact that I can’t hold a tune that’s upsetting her. I’m not saying that everything I know about parenting I learned from viral posts on the internet, but there was an illuminating tweet doing the rounds last week that said: “Today I learned if you try to sing along with a toddler when you have not been invited to do so, it is a sign of great disrespect in their culture.” I im

item.title: We’re in a flaking epidemic. No wonder no one wants to host gatherings | Chelsea Flagan
item.description: We point to self-care as we skip out on activities – but routinely staying home poses its own risk to our mental health You might have heard by now, but Americans are quite lonely , especially if they’re young. The kind of low-effort, high-frequency hanging out we used to rely on – dropping by for dinner, meeting up at the park, watching each other’s kids – has all but evaporated from our lives, leaving us unmoored from the social fabric that underpins our most basic wellbeing. (For reference, chronic loneliness has a comparable impact on long-term health to smoking .) Continue reading...

item.title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
item.description: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, at center of legal fight, says he ‘should not be unjustly accused’ because of leftwing views James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”. Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza. Continue reading...

item.title: Bill McKibben: 2027 may be the year Americans turn on fossil fuels – Stateside with Kai and Carter
item.description: It’s been another year in which the climate emergency has encroached on the lives of Americans across the country. From gigantic waves battering the California coastline to heat domes driving triple-digit temperatures in the southwest, we are reminded regularly that a crisis is here. Meanwhile, leaders gathered in Turkey for Cop31 failed to reach an agreement on how to move forward, and the US didn’t even bother to show up. To understand this moment, Kai Wright speaks to the environmentalist and author Bill McKibben about what he thinks must be done to slow the rapid advances of global heating, and what he wants to see from Democrats in 2027. Plus, he answers your questions about solar power, and how to talk to your family about the climate emergency Continue reading...

Inside, Msukwa, 25, a pregnant mother from Kasache village in central Malawi, clutches a handwritten scrap of paper instructing her to buy paracetamol from a private vendor across the road. item.title: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
item.description: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

item.title: Post your questions for Carl Cox
item.description: Ahead of him rounding out the year at a huge London show, the DJ legend will join us to answer your questions Beatifically smiling as he sends another packed dancefloor into raptures, Carl Cox is one of the most enduring and reliably euphoria-inducing figures in UK club culture history. As he prepares to close out the current season at Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, and looks towards a return of his residency at Ibiza nightclub Unvrs, he will join us to answer your questions. Known for playing a banging yet nuanced blend of house and techno, Cox’s career stretches back to the age of 10, learning his craft growing up in London and later Brighton, funding nights out by trimming his neighbours’ hedges. As Chicago house, Detroit techno and other new styles hit the UK, Cox was primed to receive them: fluidly mixing across three decks at once, he immersed himself in both the illegal rave scene and the new wave of nightclubs cropping up to showcase this music. item.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
item.description: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. item.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: lactonic scents will have you smelling like cream soda – in a good way
item.description: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. item.title: Search for next USMNT head coach needs to prioritize competence over fame
item.description: The job of Mauricio Pochettino’s successor is to fine-tune a team on the up. That requires a bureaucrat rather than a figurehead First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it. item.title: ‘Half price!’ ‘Only two left!’ How to resist the bargains you just don’t need – this Black Friday and beyond
item.description: Everywhere you look, there’s another unrepeatable deal at an unmissable price. What’s on offer will make you happier, smarter and sexier. Except, of course, it won’t. Let us help you ignore the ‘consumption noise’ The other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it.

item.title: Vaim Hotel by Jon Fosse review – not your typical ghost story
item.description: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. item.title: Blade Runner 2099 review – every scene of this TV version is packed with terrifying visual beauty
item.description: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. item.title: The story of how Pelé and Maradona went from friends to bitter rivals

Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. item.title: Secrets by Bob Woodward with Claire McMullen review – the world’s most famous reporter reveals all
item.description: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The r

item.title: ‘I was physically beating myself up before a take’: Rory Culkin on anxiety, fatherhood and his famous brothers
item.description: The star of Lords of Chaos, Scream 4 and Gabriel was always drawn to the dark side. Is that why he seems happier in Hollywood than his better-known brothers – and why he loved making Nocturne with Stephen Graham? Rory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.” I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street sa

item.title: ‘Working with Kanye West? Talk about intractable egos!’ Caroline Shaw: the Pulitzer-winning composer everyone wants to work with
item.description: She has collaborated with classical giants such as Anne Sofie von Otter – and pop stars including Phoebe Bridgers. But what happened when Caroline Shaw hit ‘peak hamster wheel’? ‘Look at those!” gasps Caroline Shaw, standing next to me at an old steelworks in Germany’s industrial heartlands. Behind us are defunct concrete cooling towers and, in front, main buildings that sprawl off in a mix of brick and corrugated iron. But Shaw is looking upwards, awed by massive exhaust pipes looming overhead. This place, in the city of Bochum in western Germany, oozes post-industrial chic. These days it’s the Jahrhunderthalle , an arts venue where Shaw is performing later with the Attacca Quartet. For now the complex is shut, so we chat on a concrete bench. Intercepting Shaw, the youngest ever winner of the Pulitzer prize for music, is no mean feat: “in demand” is an understatement for this Portland-based US composer, singer, producer, violinist and viola player. item.title: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew
item.description: Just like the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, the Brexit debate is back. The lesson here is that anything with a dodgy whiff about it will only come back Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television? Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. item.title: The Russian army’s secret death toll – podcast
item.description: Vladimir Putin has always kept the number of soldiers killed in Ukraine a secret, but at one point 720 were dying in 24 hours. Pjotr Sauer reports. Now documents leaked to the Guardian have revealed its true scale . The Guardian’s Russia affairs correspondent, Pjotr Sauer , tells Helen Pidd what reporters have discovered. item.title: Rayan Cherki magic denies Napoli but Manchester City’s struggles continue
item.description: For reasons best known to those eyeing the pound signs, Manchester City gave a debut to a special rust-coloured kit in front of a nonplussed crowd. It was of a piece with their performance for most of a familiarly frustrating night that at least concluded with a shot of energy, the home side belatedly shaking off their torpor and ending the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne. Despite the relief sparked by a fine equaliser by Rayan Cherki, who was rewarded for an insistent but hitherto fruitless evening’s endeavours when his angled shot flashed past Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, it was hard to see this as anything but a perfect snapshot of their autumn difficulties. Nobody could pretend City were up against crack opposition in a one-paced Napoli, who are eighth in Serie A and lack the brio of old, but they simply cannot keep the door shut and could not have quibbled about departing with a defeat. item.title: Dortmund’s Beier halts Arsenal charge after thunderbolt from Gyökeres
item.description: Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. item.title: Gukesh escapes time crisis to draw world chess championship opener with Sindarov
item.description: Opening game ends in draw by repetition Defending champion plays white in Game 2 Read our move-by-move report of Game 1 Sindarov: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’ Indian chess star Gukesh Dommaraju held off Javokhir Sindarov amid a mounting time crisis on Tuesday, drawing the opening game of their eagerly awaited $2.5m world title match in 38 moves at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the picturesque Geneva suburb of Cologny. After spending more than 36 minutes on a single move and much of the afternoon racing against the clock, the defending champion said the time he invested early helped him play faster as a drawish position sharpened and his minutes dwindled opposite the in-form Uzbek challenger . “When I got into the time trouble, I’d already thought about the next few moves,” Gukesh said. “And then the moves after that were pretty easy.” Continue reading...

item.description: This was Aston Villa’s third trip to Istanbul in the calendar year but, this time, they departed with different emotions. Galatasaray’s match-winner, Deniz Gul, finished with similar, the substitute requiring a bandage after bravely taking a boot to the face from Nicolas Jackson as the hosts rippled the net on 77 minutes. It was the game’s first effort on target, Galatasaray maintaining their commanding form on home soil to extend Villa’s winless run to six matches in all competitions. item.title: Their loss changed Appalachian forests for ever. Now the American chestnut is back
item.description: The trees have been functionally extinct in the US for nearly a century. But new techniques are creating plants resistant to the parasitic blight that almost wiped them out Jeff White is starstruck by a tree. The farmer and environmentalist from rural Maryland has an affinity with the American chestnut but has never seen one stretch from root to sky like this one. “About how tall is it?” he asks. “Over 70ft [21 metres],” says Cassie Stark, director of science implementation for the American Chestnut Foundation (TACF). “Just incredible,” White says, his gaze fixed upwards. “I’ve never seen one so tall and so healthy.” ‘Thompson’, above left, is an unusually tall specimen of an American chestnut, a now-rare species once ubiquitous in the US. item.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
item.description: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

item.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
item.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

The US and the UK had been publicly warning their allies for weeks about what Russia was planning, as well as threatening the Russians with a wave of sanctions unprecedented against a major power. Putin’s foreign policy had long relied on confusion and untruth. By saying that they knew exactly what he was up to, Britain and America were hoping first to deny him his usual ambiguity, and second to pressure the men around him into making him stop, since war would deprive them of the stolen assets they’d stashed in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods. item.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
item.description: Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes? In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. item.title: Why I love Rome in winter: ‘We reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines’
item.description: There is plenty of sunshine, the tourists have thinned out – and no one does a traditional Christmas like the Romans There was a time when, during a Rome winter, I would crave the warmer months. Not any more. The combination of intense heat and overtourism has made summer poco piacevole , as Italians would say – not very pleasant. So come mid-September, when the temperature drops and the crowds thin out, our mood lifts as we reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines. In winter, the temperature is mostly mild and there is still plenty of sunshine (we do tend to grumble if the rain and grey skies persist for a few days). Rome is best seen on foot, and my favourite time to walk it is on a Sunday. Until earlier this year, I lived in Esquilino, a vibrant neighbourhood close to Termini train station. I’d begin with coffee at Gatsby Cafe by Piazza Vittorio before walking along Via Merulana – a tree-lined street similar to a Parisian boulevard – and then through the Colle Oppio par

item.title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary by Anjet Daanje review – don’t miss this glorious epic inspired by Emily Brontë
item.description: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue read

item.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
item.description: Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend. Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Des

item.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
item.description: On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union. Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. item.description: The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delight As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along. César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan says when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine. Strolling in, he eases into an easier chair, golf course spreading out beyond the terrace, west of Madrid, and orders a detox almost as green. It is nearly 20 years since he played his first game and a few months since he played his last, training kit replaced by bermudas, loafers and a polo, a picture of relaxation. So what’s it like not being a footballer? “Well, different,” he says. Then he laughs, which he does a lot. It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did. And for all the self-deprecation, the lack of triumphalism, he did everything. item.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
item.description: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

item.title: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
item.description: Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years. Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. item.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
item.description: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it. But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
item.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator

item.description: In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group. As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it. Continue reading...

item.title: Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid
item.description: ‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2 . The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before. The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards. In June, the former Barcelona and Brazil legend Ronaldinho was unveiled by the Serie C side Ravenna to make his comeback at the age of 46 – 11 years after his last official game. Then silence. But on a chilly November day on the eastern coast of Italy, there he was , not only in the squad, but in the starting XI for the eagerly anticipated derby against Forlì as Ravenna chase promotion. Continue reading...

item.title: WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?
item.description: Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. item.title: Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number
item.description: Who is football’s most legendary No 9? Has there ever been a legendary No 28? And why exactly does Mario Balotelli love wearing No 45 so much? Here’s our list and the stories behind it The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure. *** Continue reading...

item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
